theme_zh: 主持新專案的啟動會議
summary_zh: 學會在專案啟動會議上說明時程、分工和下一步，並分清楚三種未來說法：已排定的安排、已決定的打算，和當下才做的決定。

vocab.definition: to start a meeting, project, or event
vocab.example: We're kicking off the new project on Monday morning.
vocab.example_zh: 我們週一早上啟動新專案。

vocab.definition: a specific piece of work that must be finished and handed over by a certain date
vocab.example: The first deliverable is a test version for the support team.
vocab.example_zh: 第一個交付成果是給客服團隊用的測試版。

vocab.zh: 範圍蔓延（需求越加越多）
vocab.definition: the slow growth of a project as people keep adding new requests
vocab.example: If we say yes to every new idea, scope creep will kill our timeline.
vocab.example_zh: 如果每個新點子都答應，需求越加越多，時程就毀了。

vocab.definition: the person who is responsible for something and whom others go to with questions
vocab.example: Jun will be the point person for the two new hires.
vocab.example_zh: Jun 會是兩位新同事的負責窗口。

vocab.definition: a rough number that is close to the real amount but not exact
vocab.example: Can you give finance a ballpark figure for the budget?
vocab.example_zh: 你可以先給財務一個預算的大概數字嗎？

vocab.definition: to gradually increase speed, effort, or ability, often at the start of something new
vocab.example: New team members usually need two weeks to ramp up.
vocab.example_zh: 新成員通常需要兩週才能上手。

vocab.zh: 簡短聯繫一下、對一下進度
vocab.definition: to talk briefly with someone to share news or check how things are going
vocab.example: Let's touch base on Friday before the meeting.
vocab.example_zh: 我們週五開會前先簡短對一下吧。

vocab.zh: 待辦事項（會議後要執行的工作）
vocab.definition: a task that someone agrees to do after a meeting
vocab.example: Let's end the meeting by going over the action items.
vocab.example_zh: 我們最後把待辦事項過一遍再散會。

reading.title: Grace's First Kickoff
paragraphs: Grace Lin has just been asked to lead her first big project: moving her company's customer support to a new online system. The kickoff meeting is on Monday at ten, and she's spent the weekend getting ready. Her manager gave her one piece of advice: "People won't remember your slides. They'll remember whether they know what to do next."

So Grace is going to keep the meeting short. She's going to kick off with the big picture: why the company is changing systems and what the new one will do for customers. Then she'll walk through the timeline. The first deliverable, a test version for the support team, is due at the end of March, and the full launch is planned for June. She doesn't have exact costs yet, so she'll give a ballpark figure and update everyone in two weeks.

She's also worried about scope creep. Every department has ideas for extra features, and if she says yes to all of them, the team will fall behind within a month. Her plan is to write down every new request and review the list with the sponsors before anyone signs off on the list.

Two engineers are joining the team late, so Grace has asked Jun, a senior developer, to be their point person and help them get up to speed. Jun agreed right away, and Grace told him, "I owe you one." She's also giving the finance team a heads-up that the budget might change.

The meeting will end with action items: who is doing what, and by when. If everyone leaves the room knowing their next step, Grace believes the project will stay on track. On Monday, she'll find out whether she's right.

questions.q: What is the new project about?
options: Hiring two engineers for the support team.
Moving customer support to a new online system.
Cutting the finance team's budget.
Designing new slides for the sales team.
questions.explain_zh: 第一段：moving her company's customer support to a new online system——專案是把客服搬到新的線上系統。

questions.q: What will Grace do with requests for extra features?
options: Say yes to all of them to keep every department happy.
Ask Jun to build them after the launch.
Write them down and review them with the sponsors before approving any.
Ignore them until the full launch in June.
questions.explain_zh: 第三段：Her plan is to write down every new request and review the list with the sponsors before anyone signs off on it——先記下來，和專案發起人一起檢視後才核准。

questions.q: Why did Grace's manager say that people won't remember her slides?
options: The manager thinks Grace's slides are not very well designed.
The manager wants her to make sure everyone leaves knowing their next step.
The manager thinks the meeting should have no slides at all.
The manager expects most people to miss the meeting.
questions.explain_zh: 推論題：主管接著說 They'll remember whether they know what to do next；最後一段 Grace 也把會議收在 action items，希望 everyone leaves the room knowing their next step。可見主管的重點是讓大家清楚下一步，而不是批評投影片。

grammar.point: Future forms: will, going to, present continuous for plans
grammar.point_zh: 未來式：will、be going to、現在進行式表示已安排的計畫

guide.key_zh: 看這件事「決定」的時間：早就排進行事曆、之前就決定了，還是說話當下才決定

uses.label_zh: 已經排進行事曆、跟人約好的安排

uses.note_zh: 時刻表（班機、會議系統排程）也可以用現在式：The meeting starts at 10.

uses.label_zh: 之前就決定的打算，或看著證據做的預測

mistakes.right: Don't worry, I'll send the slides tonight.

exercises.q: "We're out of coffee pods." — "Oh, ___ some on my way back from lunch."
options: I'll pick up
I'm picking up
I pick up
I'd pick up
exercises.explain_zh: 聽到沒咖啡膠囊，說話當下才決定順手去買 → will：I'll pick up some。I'm picking up 表示早就安排好，和「剛聽到」矛盾；I pick up 是習慣；I'd pick up 是假設語氣，要有條件才用。

exercises.q: I can't join the 3 p.m. call. I ___ (meet) the vendor at the same time — it's been in my calendar for weeks.
exercises.explain_zh: 已經排進行事曆好幾週的安排 → 現在進行式 I'm meeting 最自然；I'm going to meet 也可以。I will meet 聽起來像現在才決定，和「排了好幾週」矛盾。

exercises.q: Look at this timeline. We ___ the March deadline if we don't add another developer.
options: miss
are going to miss
are missing
would miss
exercises.explain_zh: 看著時程表（證據）做預測 → be going to：We're going to miss。說 will miss 也對。are missing 表示已排定的安排，「錯過截止日」不是會事先排好的事；would miss 是假設語氣，不能搭配 if we don't；miss 單用現在式不表示未來。

exercises.q: "Can someone send Jun the slides?" — "Sure, I ___ (send) them right now."
exercises.explain_zh: 別人一問，當下才主動答應 → will：I'll send them right now。這種「我來！」的即時決定不用 be going to 或現在進行式。

options: We kicking off the project next Monday.
We're going kick off the project next Monday.
We're kicking off the project next Monday.
We will to kick off the project next Monday.
exercises.explain_zh: 已排定的安排：be + V-ing，be 動詞（are）不能漏 → We're kicking off。be going to 的 to 不能漏；will 後面直接接原形，不加 to。

writing.task: You're leading a new project. Write a short email (80-150 words) inviting your team to the kickoff meeting. Use three short paragraphs: (1) when and where the meeting is; (2) what you're going to cover; (3) what you'd like people to do before the meeting.
writing.task_zh: 你負責一個新專案。寫一封 80–150 字的 email 邀請團隊參加啟動會議，分三小段：(1) 會議的時間地點；(2) 你打算講哪些內容；(3) 希望大家會前先做什麼。
writing.sample:
Hi team,

We're kicking off the new support system project next Monday at 10 a.m. in the big meeting room. The meeting will take about forty-five minutes.

First, I'm going to explain why we're changing systems. Then I'll walk you through the timeline. Our first deliverable is a test version for the support team, and it's due at the end of March. We'll finish with action items, so everyone will know their next step.

Before Monday, please read the one-page project summary I've attached. If you have any concerns, let's touch base on Friday. I'll be at my desk all afternoon.

Thanks, and see you on Monday!

Grace

已排定的安排用 be + V-ing（We're kicking off…）；打算用 be going to；當下的承諾或提議用 will（I'll be at my desk…）
用到 kick off（可寫 kicking off）、deliverable、touch base，總長 80–150 字
寄出前檢查：每個句子都有主詞和動詞，時間、數字都寫清楚

reading.title: Why Most Kickoffs Fail Before Day One
paragraphs: Ask any project manager about kickoff meetings and you'll hear the same complaint: they're either a pep talk with no substance or a two-hour slog through a slide deck nobody reads. Either way, people nod along, walk out, and three weeks later half of them can't say what they actually signed up for.

The problem usually starts before anyone enters the room. The sponsors haven't agreed on what success looks like, so the project lead papers over the gaps with vague phrases like "improve the customer experience." Everyone hears what they want to hear. Marketing assumes the new system will capture more data; support assumes it'll cut response times; finance assumes it won't cost a cent more than last year. Nobody is lying, but they're not on the same page either.

Experienced leads drag these conflicts into the open early. A week before the kickoff, they sit down with each sponsor one-on-one and ask a blunt question: "If this project goes well, what will be different in six months?" The answers rarely match, and that's the point. It's far cheaper to hash out a disagreement over coffee than to discover it in month four, when half the budget is already spent.

The meeting itself then has a narrower job. Instead of selling the vision, it confirms decisions that have already been made, flags the risks that are still open, and ends with names next to tasks. Some leads go further and close with a "pre-mortem": they ask the team to imagine it's a year from now and the project has failed, then list the most likely reasons why. It sounds gloomy, but people who would never criticize a plan in public are surprisingly willing to explain how it might go wrong.

questions.q: According to the writer, why do different groups often leave a kickoff with different expectations?
options: The slide deck was too long for anyone to read.
The goals were described so vaguely that each group interpreted them differently.
The project lead deliberately gave each sponsor false information.
Finance refused to share the budget with the other teams.
questions.explain_zh: 第二段：project lead papers over the gaps with vague phrases… Everyone hears what they want to hear——目標講得太模糊，各部門各自解讀。文中明說 Nobody is lying，所以不是故意騙人。

questions.q: Why does the writer say that the sponsors' answers not matching is "the point"?
options: The lead wants to prove that the sponsors are wrong.
Mismatched answers mean the project should be cancelled.
The one-on-ones are meant to bring out disagreements early, while they're cheap to fix.
Sponsors are expected to change their minds after the kickoff.
questions.explain_zh: 推論題：緊接著說 It's far cheaper to hash out a disagreement over coffee than to discover it in month four——一對一面談的目的就是提早把分歧挖出來，趁還便宜時解決。

questions.q: What does the writer imply is the main benefit of a pre-mortem?
options: It lets people raise concerns they might otherwise keep to themselves.
It makes the meeting shorter and more cheerful.
It helps the lead decide who to blame if the project fails.
It replaces the need for one-on-one meetings with sponsors.
questions.explain_zh: 推論題：最後一句 people who would never criticize a plan in public are surprisingly willing to explain how it might go wrong——平常不敢公開批評的人，透過「假設已經失敗」反而願意說出風險。文中說它 sounds gloomy，所以不是讓會議更愉快。

listening.title: One Blunt Question

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Mark
lines.text: So, Grace, you wanted to talk before Monday?

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Grace
lines.text: Yes, thanks for making time. I'm meeting each sponsor this week, and I've got one question for everyone.

lines.name: Mark

lines.name: Grace
